---
title: "P3 exercises — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget"
---

The questions follow the [tutorial](index.qmd) and [slides](lec.qmd). Answer
each question before opening its answer.

## Light reactions

### 1.1

Complete the table.

| | Light reactions | Calvin–Benson cycle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Location in the chloroplast | | |
| Inputs | | |
| Outputs | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| | Light reactions | Calvin–Benson cycle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Location in the chloroplast | Thylakoid membranes | Stroma |
| Inputs | Light, H₂O, ADP + Pᵢ, NADP⁺ | CO₂, ATP, NADPH |
| Outputs | O₂, ATP, NADPH | Triose phosphate (sugars), ADP + Pᵢ, NADP⁺ |
:::

### 1.2

The O₂ released in photosynthesis comes from:

a. CO₂
b. H₂O
c. glucose
d. ribulose 1,5-bisphosphate

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

b. Water is oxidised at photosystem II, supplying electrons and releasing O₂.
CO₂ supplies the carbon of the sugars.
:::

### 1.3

Put the carriers of linear (non-cyclic) electron flow in order, starting with
water: ferredoxin, photosystem I, plastoquinone, NADP⁺, photosystem II,
plastocyanin, cytochrome *b*₆*f* complex.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

H₂O → photosystem II → plastoquinone → cytochrome *b*₆*f* complex →
plastocyanin → photosystem I → ferredoxin → NADP⁺ (via
ferredoxin–NADP⁺ reductase).
:::

### 1.4

Complete the table comparing linear and cyclic electron flow (yes/no).

| | Linear flow | Cyclic flow |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Photosystem II involved | | |
| O₂ released | | |
| NADPH formed | | |
| ATP formed | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| | Linear flow | Cyclic flow |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Photosystem II involved | Yes | No |
| O₂ released | Yes | No |
| NADPH formed | Yes | No |
| ATP formed | Yes | Yes |
:::

### 1.5

How is the energy of the proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane used,
and in which direction do protons flow through the enzyme?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

ATP synthase uses it to make ATP from ADP and Pᵢ. Protons flow from the
thylakoid lumen (high H⁺) to the stroma (low H⁺), so ATP is formed in the
stroma.
:::

## The Calvin–Benson cycle and photorespiration

### 2.1

Name the three phases of the Calvin–Benson cycle in order, and the enzyme that
catalyses the first.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Carboxylation → reduction → regeneration of ribulose 1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP).
Carboxylation is catalysed by Rubisco (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate
carboxylase/oxygenase), which adds CO₂ to RuBP to form two molecules of
3-phosphoglycerate.
:::

### 2.2

Fixing 3 CO₂ into one net triose phosphate requires 9 ATP and 6 NADPH.

a. How much ATP and NADPH are needed to fix 6 CO₂, the carbon of one hexose?
b. What is the ATP : NADPH ratio required?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.
b. 3 : 2 (1.5 ATP per NADPH).
:::

### 2.3

True or false? Correct any false statements.

a. The Calvin–Benson cycle runs all night because it is a "dark reaction".
b. Rubisco can react with O₂ as well as CO₂.
c. Photorespiration is the same process as mitochondrial respiration.
d. Photorespiration releases CO₂ that has already been fixed.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. False. The cycle needs ATP and NADPH from the light reactions, and several
   of its enzymes are activated in light; it stops soon after darkness begins.
b. True.
c. False. Photorespiration starts with Rubisco oxygenation and recycles
   2-phosphoglycolate; mitochondrial respiration oxidises sugars to make ATP.
d. True. CO₂ is released in the mitochondria when glycine is converted to
   serine.
:::

### 2.4

Name the three organelles involved in the photorespiratory pathway.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Chloroplast, peroxisome and mitochondrion.
:::

### 2.5

State whether each change increases or decreases the rate of
photorespiration relative to carboxylation in a C3 leaf.

a. Higher leaf temperature
b. Stomatal closure during drought
c. Higher atmospheric CO₂ concentration

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Increases (the solubility of CO₂ falls more than that of O₂, and Rubisco's
   specificity for CO₂ decreases).
b. Increases (the CO₂ concentration inside the leaf falls).
c. Decreases.
:::

## C3, C4 and CAM

### 3.1

Complete the table.

| | C3 | C4 | CAM |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Enzyme of initial CO₂ fixation | | | |
| First stable product | | | |
| Separation of initial fixation and Calvin cycle | | | |
| Stomata open mainly | | | |
| Photorespiration | | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| | C3 | C4 | CAM |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Enzyme of initial CO₂ fixation | Rubisco | PEP carboxylase | PEP carboxylase |
| First stable product | 3-phosphoglycerate (3 C) | Oxaloacetate (4 C) | Oxaloacetate (4 C), stored as malate |
| Separation of initial fixation and Calvin cycle | None | Spatial: mesophyll and bundle-sheath cells | Temporal: night and day |
| Stomata open mainly | Day | Day | Night |
| Photorespiration | High in warm conditions | Low | Low |

In all three, the CO₂ is finally fixed by Rubisco in the Calvin–Benson cycle.
:::

### 3.2

Classify each plant as C3, C4 or CAM: maize, wheat, pineapple, sugarcane,
rice, prickly pear cactus (*Opuntia*).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

C3: wheat, rice. C4: maize, sugarcane. CAM: pineapple, *Opuntia*.
:::

### 3.3

Which observation is characteristic of a CAM plant?

a. Bundle-sheath cells packed with chloroplasts
b. Acidity of the leaf tissue rises during the night and falls during the day
c. Stomata open only at midday
d. Rubisco is absent

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

b. Malic acid accumulates in the vacuole at night and is decarboxylated during
the day to supply CO₂ to Rubisco. Option a describes C4 (Kranz) anatomy.
:::

### 3.4

Name the advantage and the cost of the C4 CO₂-concentrating mechanism.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Advantage: high CO₂ around Rubisco in the bundle sheath suppresses
photorespiration, giving higher photosynthesis and water-use efficiency in
warm, bright conditions. Cost: extra ATP (2 ATP per CO₂) to regenerate
PEP from pyruvate.
:::

## Light-response curves and units

### 4.1

The net CO₂ exchange of one leaf is measured at four light levels. Positive
values are net uptake.

| Light (µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹) | Net CO₂ exchange (µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹) |
| ---: | ---: |
| 0 | −2 |
| 50 | 0 |
| 200 | 6 |
| 800 | 9 |

a. What is the rate of respiration in darkness?
b. What is the light compensation point?
c. Calculate the increase in net CO₂ uptake per additional µmol photons
   between 50 and 200, and between 200 and 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹.
d. Assuming respiration is unchanged in light, what is gross photosynthesis at
   200 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. 2 µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹.
b. 50 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹, where net exchange is zero.
c. 6 / 150 = 0.04 µmol CO₂ per µmol photons; 3 / 600 = 0.005 µmol CO₂ per
   µmol photons. The response saturates at high light.
d. 6 + 2 = 8 µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹.
:::

### 4.2

A leaf of area 0.02 m² takes up CO₂ at a constant net rate of
6 µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹ for 10 min.

a. Calculate the total net CO₂ uptake in µmol.
b. Convert it to mg CO₂ (M(CO₂) = 44 g mol⁻¹).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. 6 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹ × 0.02 m² × 600 s = 72 µmol CO₂.
b. 72 × 10⁻⁶ mol × 44 g mol⁻¹ = 3.2 × 10⁻³ g = 3.2 mg CO₂.
:::

## Sources, sinks and phloem transport

### 5.1

Classify each organ as a source or a sink.

a. Mature, illuminated leaf
b. Developing fruit
c. Root tip
d. Young, expanding leaf
e. Potato tuber sprouting in spring

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Source. b. Sink. c. Sink. d. Sink. e. Source (stored starch is mobilised
to supply the new shoot).
:::

### 5.2

Put the steps of the pressure-flow model of phloem transport in order:

a. hydrostatic pressure rises in the sieve tubes at the source
b. sucrose is loaded into the sieve-element–companion-cell complex
c. sucrose is unloaded at the sink and water leaves the sieve tubes
d. water enters the sieve tubes from the xylem by osmosis
e. sap moves by bulk flow towards the sink

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

b → d → a → e → c.
:::

### 5.3

Name the main sugar transported in the phloem of most plants and the main
storage carbohydrate in chloroplasts.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Sucrose is transported in the phloem; starch is stored in chloroplasts.
:::

## Respiration and nitrogen assimilation

### 6.1

Complete the table for aerobic respiration.

| Stage | Location | Main products |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Glycolysis | | |
| Tricarboxylic acid (citric acid) cycle | | |
| Electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| Stage | Location | Main products |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Glycolysis | Cytosol (and plastids) | Pyruvate, ATP, NADH |
| Tricarboxylic acid (citric acid) cycle | Mitochondrial matrix | CO₂, NADH, FADH₂, ATP |
| Electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation | Inner mitochondrial membrane | ATP, H₂O (O₂ is the final electron acceptor) |
:::

### 6.2

Roots of a flooded plant switch to fermentation.

a. Why can glycolysis continue during fermentation?
b. Name the main fermentation products in plant roots.
c. About how many ATP are formed per glucose by fermentation, compared with
   complete aerobic oxidation?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Fermentation regenerates NAD⁺ from NADH, which glycolysis requires.
b. Ethanol and CO₂ (and some lactate).
c. 2 ATP per glucose by fermentation, compared with about 30 ATP by aerobic
   respiration.
:::

### 6.3

Put the steps of nitrate assimilation in order and name the enzyme for each
step: ammonium → glutamine; nitrite → ammonium; nitrate → nitrite;
glutamine + 2-oxoglutarate → glutamate.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

1. Nitrate → nitrite: nitrate reductase (cytosol).
2. Nitrite → ammonium: nitrite reductase (plastid).
3. Ammonium + glutamate → glutamine: glutamine synthetase (GS).
4. Glutamine + 2-oxoglutarate → 2 glutamate: glutamate synthase (GOGAT).

The reducing power, ATP and carbon skeletons (2-oxoglutarate) come from
photosynthesis and respiration, so nitrogen assimilation depends on carbon
metabolism.
:::

## Explore: Light-response curve {#explore-p3-lightcurve}

The demo plots net CO₂ uptake of one sun leaf against light, for a C3 leaf
(wheat) or a C4 leaf (maize). Use the Light slider (or drag the round handle)
to read the curve; the table gives net and gross photosynthesis, dark
respiration, the CO₂ released by photorespiration, the light compensation
point and what limits the rate. The scenario buttons ("Hot, dry", "1000 ppm",
"Cool, 12 °C") change CO₂, temperature and stomata but keep the light where it
is. Press Reset before each question.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="p3-lightcurve" data-pathway="C3" data-co2="420" data-temp="25" data-light="600"></div>
<script src="../../demos/dist/p3-lightcurve.js"></script>
```

### E1.1

Start values: C3 leaf, 420 ppm CO₂, 25 °C, light 600 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹.

a. Read off net uptake, gross photosynthesis and dark respiration. Show that
   the three numbers are consistent.
b. What limits the rate at this light: light or Rubisco?
c. Move the light to 0. What is the net uptake now, and why is it negative?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Net 14.7, gross 15.9 and respiration 1.2 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹. Net = gross −
   respiration: 15.9 − 1.2 = 14.7.
b. Light. At 2000 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ the limit switches to Rubisco
   (net about 16), where the curve flattens.
c. −1.2 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹. In darkness there is no photosynthesis, but
   mitochondrial respiration continues and releases CO₂.
:::

### E1.2

Tick "Zoom in on low light". Read off the light compensation point of the C3
leaf at 25 °C, then press "C4 leaf (maize)" and read it again. Which leaf has
the lower compensation point, and by about how much?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

C3: 25 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹. C4: 23 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹. The two are almost
the same: at 25 °C both leaves have the same dark respiration (1.2), and at
low light the C4 leaf's extra ATP cost per CO₂ roughly cancels the C3 leaf's
loss to photorespiration.
:::

### E1.3

Reset (C3, light 600) and press "Hot, dry" (38 °C, stomata nearly closed).

a. Read off net uptake, the CO₂ released by photorespiration (with the
   number of O₂ fixed per CO₂) and dark respiration. Compare with E1.1.
b. Now press "C4 leaf (maize)" and "Hot, dry" again. What is the net uptake
   of the C4 leaf?
c. Which enzyme explains the difference between b and a?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Net uptake falls from 14.7 to 1.5 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹. Photorespiration rises
   from 2.7 to 5.4 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹ (O₂/CO₂ from 0.29 to 1.10), and respiration
   rises from 1.2 to 3.0. Closed stomata lower the CO₂ inside the leaf, and
   heat raises Rubisco's oxygenation relative to carboxylation.
b. 13.8 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹, about nine times the C3 leaf.
c. PEP carboxylase. It does not react with O₂ and binds CO₂ (as HCO₃⁻) at
   low concentration, so the C4 leaf concentrates CO₂ around Rubisco in the
   bundle sheath and photorespiration stays near zero (0.3).
:::

### E1.4

Reset and press "1000 ppm" (a greenhouse with CO₂ enrichment), light 600.

a. Read off net uptake and photorespiration of the C3 leaf.
b. Press "C4 leaf (maize)". Does raising CO₂ from 420 to 1000 ppm increase
   the net uptake of the C4 leaf at this light?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Net 18.9 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹ (up from 14.7); photorespiration 1.3 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹
   (down from 2.7; O₂/CO₂ 0.12). More CO₂ wins the competition with O₂ at
   Rubisco's active site.
b. No: it stays at 29.7 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹, because the C4 leaf already
   concentrates CO₂ and is light-limited at 600. This is why CO₂ enrichment
   benefits C3 crops more than C4 crops.
:::

### E1.5

Reset and press "Cool, 12 °C" (light 600). Read off net uptake for the C3 leaf,
then press "C4 leaf (maize)" and "Cool, 12 °C". Which leaf takes up more CO₂,
and what limits the C4 leaf?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

C3: 10.1 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹. C4: 6.0 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹. The C3 leaf wins. The C4 leaf
is limited by enzyme capacity: its enzymes are cold-sensitive, and it pays
2 extra ATP per CO₂, which is not worth it when photorespiration is already
low in the cold (C3 O₂/CO₂ is only 0.15 at 12 °C). This is why C4 grasses
dominate warm regions and C3 grasses cool ones.
:::
